Students at restricting schools reported spending an average of 18 more minutes per day talking face to face with peers than students at the other schools. Loneliness was measured with a six-item self-report scale, scored from 6 to 24. We did not observe students directly and did not collect data on phone use outside school.

The restricting schools were smaller on average, with a mean enrollment of 410 students, compared with 610 at the comparison schools.

Students who reported more face-to-face conversation also reported slightly lower loneliness, but this correlation was weak (r = -0.12).

Second, only 13.5% of invited students responded, and students who chose to respond may differ from those who did not. Third, the six schools were in a single state, so the results may not apply elsewhere. Fourth, because we surveyed students at one point in time, we cannot say whether conversation changed after the restrictions began. A study that measured the same students before and after a restriction would be needed to test whether restrictions cause more conversation.

In this sample, whole-day phone restrictions were associated with more self-reported face-to-face conversation but not with lower loneliness. Further research with stronger designs is needed.

We surveyed 412 students at six public high schools in one Midwestern state during the spring semester. Three schools restricted phone use for the whole school day; three allowed phones at lunch. Students at restricting schools reported spending an average of 18 more minutes per day talking face to face with peers than students at the other schools. We found no difference in self-reported loneliness between the two groups. Because the design is cross-sectional, these results describe an association and cannot show that the restrictions caused the difference.

Methods
Participants. We invited all students in grades 10 through 12 at the six schools to complete an online survey. Participation was voluntary, and 412 of 3,050 invited students (13.5%) responded. Respondents were 58% female and 42% male.

Measures. The survey asked students to estimate how many minutes they spent talking face to face with other students during a typical school day, including lunch and passing periods. Loneliness was measured with a six-item self-report scale, scored from 6 to 24. We did not observe students directly and did not collect data on phone use outside school.

Schools. The three restricting schools required phones to be stored in lockers from the first bell to the last bell. The three comparison schools allowed phones at lunch and between classes. The restricting schools were smaller on average, with a mean enrollment of 410 students, compared with 610 at the comparison schools.

Results
Students at restricting schools reported a mean of 64 minutes of face-to-face conversation per school day, compared with 46 minutes at comparison schools, a difference of 18 minutes. Mean loneliness scores were 13.1 at restricting schools and 13.4 at comparison schools, a difference that was not statistically significant. Students who reported more face-to-face conversation also reported slightly lower loneliness, but this correlation was weak (r = -0.12).

Discussion
Students at schools that restricted phones for the whole day said they talked with each other more. This pattern fits the idea that removing phones leaves more room for conversation. However, the schools were not randomly assigned to restrict phones, and they differed in other ways, including size. Smaller schools may simply offer more chances for students to know each other.

Limitations
This study has several limitations. First, all measures were self-reported, and students may overestimate or underestimate their conversation time. Second, only 13.5% of invited students responded, and students who chose to respond may differ from those who did not. Third, the six schools were in a single state, so the results may not apply elsewhere. Fourth, because we surveyed students at one point in time, we cannot say whether conversation changed after the restrictions began. A study that measured the same students before and after a restriction would be needed to test whether restrictions cause more conversation.

Conclusion
In this sample, whole-day phone restrictions were associated with more self-reported face-to-face conversation but not with lower loneliness. Further research with stronger designs is needed.
